subtopic_detail: choosing smoking cessation pharmacotherapy for a heavily dependent smoker with treated depression and a previous failed nicotine patch attempt
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 48-year-old man who wants to stop smoking. He has smoked 25 cigarettes a day since he was 17 and lights his first within five minutes of waking.

He made one attempt two years ago using a 21 mg nicotine patch alone and relapsed at day four with strong cravings, particularly in the evenings. He has major depressive disorder that has been stable for three years on sertraline 100 mg daily, with no hospital admissions and no self harm. He drinks two standard drinks most nights and has no other substance use. He has no seizure history, no eating disorder, and his renal function is within normal limits. He is motivated and has set a quit date in three weeks time, and he asks what will give him the best chance this time.

data_table.Smoking history: 25 cigarettes daily for 31 years, first cigarette within 5 minutes of waking, one previous attempt with patch monotherapy relapsing at day 4
data_table.Mental health: Major depressive disorder stable for 3 years on sertraline 100 mg daily, no admissions or self harm
data_table.Investigations: Renal and liver function within normal limits

lead_in: Which pharmacotherapy would you recommend as first line for this quit attempt?

options.text: Varenicline commenced one week before the quit date and continued for twelve weeks
options.rationale: Varenicline is the single most effective agent for cessation and outperforms both patch monotherapy and bupropion in head to head trials, and the large randomised safety trial found no excess of neuropsychiatric events in people with stable treated psychiatric illness. His high dependence and previous patch failure both argue for the most effective option rather than a repeat of what did not work. (Source: RACGP: Supporting Smoking Cessation)

options.text: A 21 mg nicotine patch commenced on the quit date and continued for twelve weeks
options.rationale: Repeating patch monotherapy repeats the regimen that already failed him, and a patch alone does not address the acute evening cravings that broke the previous attempt. If nicotine replacement is chosen it should be combination therapy, patch plus a fast acting form, which is the near pair distinction here. (Source: RACGP: Supporting Smoking Cessation)

options.text: Bupropion commenced one week before the quit date and continued for twelve weeks
options.rationale: Bupropion is an effective second line agent but is less effective than varenicline, lowers the seizure threshold, and carries a serotonergic interaction risk when added to an established selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor. It would be a reasonable choice if varenicline were contraindicated or not tolerated. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Smoking Cessation)

options.text: Nicotine lozenges used on demand for cravings without any scheduled background therapy
options.rationale: Oral nicotine used alone delivers erratic blood levels and does not suppress the background withdrawal that drives relapse in the first week, so it is used as the rapid acting partner to a patch rather than as monotherapy. In a smoker of this dependence it under-treats the problem. (Source: RACGP: Supporting Smoking Cessation)

options.text: Increasing the sertraline to 150 mg daily as antidepressants also assist smoking cessation
options.rationale: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors have no cessation efficacy, and increasing a dose that is currently maintaining remission risks destabilising mood for no benefit. The antidepressant with a cessation indication is bupropion, which works through dopaminergic and noradrenergic mechanisms rather than serotonergic ones. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Smoking rates among people with mental illness remain roughly double those in the general population, and tobacco related disease accounts for a large share of the reduced life expectancy in this group, so cessation is one of the highest value interventions in psychiatric care. Concerns about neuropsychiatric harm from varenicline led to a black box warning that was later removed after a large randomised trial found no excess of serious neuropsychiatric events compared with patch or placebo, including in people with stable psychiatric disorders. Effectiveness ranks varenicline highest, followed by combination nicotine replacement, then bupropion or single form nicotine replacement. Every pharmacotherapy should be paired with behavioural support, since combining the two roughly doubles quit rates compared with either alone. Smoking induces the cytochrome P450 1A2 enzyme, so stopping raises levels of clozapine and olanzapine and these need dose review at cessation.
key_points: Varenicline is the most effective single agent and is started one to two weeks before the quit date.
Stable treated psychiatric illness is not a contraindication to varenicline.
Nicotine replacement works best as a combination of patch plus a rapid acting form.
Pair every pharmacotherapy with behavioural support such as the national quitline.
Time to first cigarette within 30 minutes of waking is the best single marker of high dependence.
explanation.pearls: Stopping smoking removes the cytochrome P450 1A2 induction that tobacco smoke produces, so clozapine levels can rise by 50 per cent or more within one to two weeks of quitting and the dose usually needs reducing with level monitoring.

subtopic_detail: responding to a rising thyroid stimulating hormone on long term lithium in a patient whose mood has been stable for years
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in a community clinic reviewing a 42-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder who has taken lithium carbonate for nine years. She has had no mood episode in seven years and works full time.

She mentions over the past four months she has felt the cold more than her colleagues, has gained 5 kg without changing her eating, and finds herself constipated. She has not felt low in mood, has slept normally and has kept up her usual activities and interests. Her routine monitoring bloods today show a lithium level of 0.72 mmol/L (0.6 to 0.8) taken twelve hours post dose, a thyroid stimulating hormone of 11.4 mIU/L (0.4 to 4.0) with a free thyroxine of 9.8 pmol/L (10 to 26), a creatinine of 76 micromol/L (45 to 90) and a corrected calcium of 2.44 mmol/L (2.15 to 2.60). Her previous thyroid stimulating hormone twelve months ago was 3.1 mIU/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 58, blood pressure 118/76, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 98 per cent in air, temperature 36.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Small diffuse non tender goitre, dry skin, delayed relaxation of the ankle reflexes, no tremor
data_table.Investigations: Lithium 0.72 mmol/L (0.6 to 0.8), thyroid stimulating hormone 11.4 mIU/L (0.4 to 4.0), free thyroxine 9.8 pmol/L (10 to 26), creatinine 76 micromol/L (45 to 90), corrected calcium 2.44 mmol/L (2.15 to 2.60)
data_table.History: Thyroid stimulating hormone 3.1 mIU/L twelve months ago, no mood episode for seven years

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer for thyroid ultrasound and fine needle aspiration of the goitre before commencing treatment
options.rationale: A small diffuse non tender goitre with biochemical hypothyroidism needs no imaging, and aspiration is reserved for a discrete nodule or features suspicious for malignancy. Imaging would delay replacement that is already clearly indicated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Continue lithium at the current dose and start thyroxine, titrating to the thyroid stimulating hormone
options.rationale: Lithium associated hypothyroidism is treated by adding thyroxine rather than by stopping a mood stabiliser that has kept her well for seven years, since the thyroid effect is fully correctable while the relapse risk on withdrawal is not. Her free thyroxine is below range with symptoms, which makes this overt rather than subclinical disease and removes any argument for observation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Cease lithium and switch to sodium valproate, then recheck thyroid function in three months
options.rationale: Stopping lithium after nine years of stability carries a substantial relapse risk, and abrupt discontinuation in particular is associated with rebound mania. Valproate is also a poor choice for a woman of reproductive age given its teratogenicity, and none of this is necessary for a treatable side effect. (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Reduce the lithium dose to achieve a level near 0.4 mmol/L and repeat thyroid function in six weeks
options.rationale: The thyroid effect is not dose dependent in a way that a modest reduction reverses, and dropping below the therapeutic range trades a correctable hormone deficiency for a loss of prophylactic efficacy. This is the near pair error of treating a side effect by under-dosing rather than by adding replacement. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Repeat the thyroid function tests in three months before starting any treatment or making changes
options.rationale: Watchful repeat testing is the correct approach to an isolated mildly raised thyroid stimulating hormone with a normal free thyroxine and no symptoms. She has a free thyroxine below the reference range together with cold intolerance, weight gain, constipation and delayed reflex relaxation, which is overt hypothyroidism. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Lithium remains the most effective long term prophylactic agent in bipolar disorder and is the only mood stabiliser with consistent evidence for reducing suicide, so preserving it through manageable side effects is usually the right trade. It interferes with thyroid hormone release from the gland and with iodine organification, producing goitre in up to 40 per cent of long term users and hypothyroidism in roughly one in five, with women over 45 and those with positive thyroid peroxidase antibodies at highest risk. Standard monitoring is a lithium level with renal function, thyroid function and calcium every three to six months, with more frequent levels after any dose change or intercurrent illness. Lithium also causes hyperparathyroidism with hypercalcaemia, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, and a slow decline in glomerular filtration rate over decades. Hypothyroidism is corrected with thyroxine while lithium continues, and the mood picture must be reviewed at the same time because hypothyroidism can itself mimic or precipitate a depressive episode.
key_points: Lithium causes hypothyroidism in roughly 20 per cent of long term users and goitre in up to 40 per cent.
Treat with thyroxine and continue lithium rather than stopping an effective mood stabiliser.
Monitor lithium level, renal function, thyroid function and calcium every three to six months.
Abrupt lithium discontinuation carries a particular risk of rebound mania.
Lithium associated hyperparathyroidism produces hypercalcaemia with an inappropriately normal or raised parathyroid hormone.
explanation.pearls: Non steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors and thiazide diuretics all reduce renal lithium clearance and can raise the level by 25 to 60 per cent within a week, so any new prescription in these classes warrants a level check at seven days.

sources.label: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

subtopic_detail: advising an adult newly started on a stimulant about driving obligations and dose timing for shift work
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 27-year-old man four weeks after starting methylphenidate for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder diagnosed this year. He reports better focus at work, is sleeping adequately, and has had no appetite loss beyond a mild reduction at lunch.

He drives a courier van for a living on a commercial licence and works rotating shifts including a night shift block every third week. He asks whether he has to tell anyone about the medication, and says a workmate told him that being on a stimulant would cost him his licence. He has no history of substance misuse, no cardiac symptoms, and no family history of sudden cardiac death. His blood pressure today is 128/78 with a pulse of 82, unchanged from baseline, and his weight is stable.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82, blood pressure 128/78, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99 per cent in air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: No tremor, normal cardiovascular examination, weight unchanged from baseline
data_table.Treatment: Methylphenidate started 4 weeks ago with symptomatic improvement and adequate sleep
data_table.Occupation: Commercial licence courier driver on rotating shifts including night shift every third week

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice about his driving?

options.text: Notification is only required if he has a crash or receives an infringement while taking the medication
options.rationale: The duty to notify arises when the condition is diagnosed or the treatment begins, not retrospectively after an adverse event. Waiting for a crash inverts the purpose of the standards, which exist to prevent one. (Source: Austroads: Assessing Fitness to Drive)

options.text: He should switch to atomoxetine, since non stimulant treatment removes any notification requirement
options.rationale: The notifiable matter is the underlying condition and its effect on driving, so changing drug class does not remove the obligation, and atomoxetine is less effective than a stimulant for most patients. Switching a treatment that is working would trade efficacy for a regulatory benefit that does not exist. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: He must notify the driver licensing authority, and treated stable illness is generally compatible with driving
options.rationale: Australian fitness to drive standards place the obligation on the driver to notify the licensing authority of a condition likely to affect driving, and for a commercial licence the standards are stricter and require periodic review. Neither the diagnosis nor stimulant treatment disqualifies him, and treatment of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder reduces rather than increases crash risk. (Source: Austroads: Assessing Fitness to Drive)

options.text: No notification is required because stimulant medication is prescribed and lawfully obtained
options.rationale: Lawful prescription addresses the question of whether he is impaired by an illicit drug but does not remove the separate obligation to notify a condition relevant to driving. The near pair distinction is between drug driving law and fitness to drive standards, which are two different frameworks. (Source: Austroads: Assessing Fitness to Drive)

options.text: He should stop driving commercially while taking any stimulant and change to a private licence
options.rationale: Blanket exclusion from commercial driving is not what the standards require, and it would impose a serious occupational penalty for a treatment that improves driving performance. Conditional licensing with periodic review is the mechanism the standards actually use. (Source: Austroads: Assessing Fitness to Drive)

explanation.summary: Adult attention deficit hyperactivity disorder is increasingly recognised in Australia and stimulant prescribing is governed by state and territory authority requirements, with most jurisdictions requiring a specialist to initiate treatment. Untreated symptoms are associated with a measurably higher motor vehicle crash rate, and pharmacological treatment reduces it, so the safety argument generally favours treating rather than withholding. Fitness to drive is assessed under the national standards, which distinguish private from commercial licences and use conditional licences with review intervals rather than outright exclusion for most treated conditions. The legal duty to notify the licensing authority rests with the driver, while the doctor's duty is to advise clearly and document that advice, with a discretionary power to report directly where a patient continues to drive against advice. Shift work adds a separate consideration, since sleep deprivation impairs driving independently of any medication and stimulant timing must not be used to mask fatigue.
key_points: The driver holds the legal obligation to notify; the doctor's obligation is to advise and document.
Commercial licence standards are stricter and typically require periodic medical review.
Treated attention deficit hyperactivity disorder is associated with a lower crash risk than untreated illness.
Baseline and follow up blood pressure, pulse, weight and sleep are the core monitoring parameters on stimulants.
Sleep deprivation from shift work impairs driving independently of medication and must be addressed separately.
explanation.pearls: Immediate release methylphenidate has a duration of roughly three to four hours while modified release preparations last eight to twelve, so a late afternoon dose taken to cover a night shift will delay sleep onset well past the end of that shift and is the usual reason a shift worker reports insomnia on stimulants.

subtopic_detail: identifying the medication cause of a low sodium in an older adult started on an antidepressant three weeks earlier
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 76-year-old woman in a community clinic. Sertraline 50 mg daily was started three weeks ago for a first episode of major depression following her husband's death, and her daughter has brought her in because she seems more muddled than before rather than less.

Her daughter says she has been unsteady, called her granddaughter by the wrong name twice, and had a fall against the doorframe on Tuesday without losing consciousness. Her mood is unchanged and she denies any thoughts of self harm. Her other medications are perindopril, which she has taken for six years without a dose change, and paracetamol as required. She has not been vomiting or had diarrhoea, has been drinking her usual four cups of tea a day, and looks euvolaemic with moist mucous membranes, no postural drop and no oedema.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76, blood pressure 132/78 with no postural drop, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 97 per cent in air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Euvolaemic with moist mucous membranes and no oedema, unsteady gait, abbreviated mental test score 6 out of 10 against 9 out of 10 one month ago
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 119 mmol/L (135 to 145), potassium 4.2 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.5), creatinine 72 micromol/L (45 to 90), serum osmolality 248 mOsm/kg (275 to 295), urine osmolality 468 mOsm/kg, urine sodium 52 mmol/L, thyroid function and morning cortisol within normal limits
data_table.Medications: Sertraline 50 mg daily started 3 weeks ago, perindopril unchanged for 6 years, paracetamol as required

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue sertraline, give intravenous sodium chloride 0.9 per cent and recheck the sodium in 24 hours
options.rationale: Isotonic saline in inappropriate antidiuresis can paradoxically lower the sodium further, because the kidney excretes the salt while retaining the water, and it leaves the causative drug in place. Volume expansion is the treatment for hypovolaemic hyponatraemia, which her euvolaemia and high urine sodium exclude. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Switch to mirtazapine at the same visit and continue the current fluid intake unchanged
options.rationale: Mirtazapine is a reasonable later choice because it carries a lower risk of this complication, but starting it at the same visit confuses the picture and does nothing about the water retention already present. Correct the sodium first, then reintroduce an antidepressant with monitoring. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Arrange computed tomography of the head for the confusion before altering any medication
options.rationale: Imaging is warranted where a fall with head strike is accompanied by focal signs, anticoagulation or a reduced conscious level, and it may still be arranged here, but it does not explain a sodium of 119 mmol/L and delays treatment of a reversible cause. The confusion and unsteadiness are fully accounted for by the hyponatraemia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Cease sertraline, restrict fluid intake and recheck the sodium within 24 to 48 hours
options.rationale: The biochemistry shows a euvolaemic hypotonic hyponatraemia with inappropriately concentrated urine and a urine sodium above 30 mmol/L, which is the pattern of inappropriate antidiuresis, and the temporal link to a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor started three weeks ago identifies the cause. Withdrawing the drug with fluid restriction corrects most cases within days, and close rechecking is needed because over rapid correction risks osmotic demyelination. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Continue sertraline, cease perindopril and recheck the sodium within 24 to 48 hours
options.rationale: Angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors can contribute to low sodium, which makes this a genuine competing culprit, but she has taken perindopril unchanged for six years while the sertraline was introduced three weeks before the sodium fell. Temporal association points to the new agent rather than the long standing one. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Antidepressants)

explanation.summary: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors are the commonest drug cause of hyponatraemia in older adults, with risk highest in the first four weeks of treatment and rising with age, female sex, low body weight, and concurrent diuretics or angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors. The mechanism is inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion, producing a euvolaemic hypotonic hyponatraemia with urine that is inappropriately concentrated and a urine sodium above 30 mmol per litre. The presentation is easily misread as a worsening of the depression being treated, or as emerging dementia, because it produces confusion, unsteadiness, falls and lethargy rather than anything obviously biochemical. Management is withdrawal of the offending drug with fluid restriction for mild to moderate cases, reserving hypertonic saline for seizures or a markedly reduced conscious level. Correction should not exceed 8 to 10 mmol per litre in 24 hours because of the risk of osmotic demyelination, and the sodium should be rechecked within a fortnight whenever a serotonergic antidepressant is restarted in an older patient.
key_points: Risk is greatest in the first four weeks after starting a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor.
Look for euvolaemia, serum osmolality below 275, urine osmolality above 100 and urine sodium above 30 mmol/L.
Exclude hypothyroidism and adrenal insufficiency before attributing the picture to inappropriate antidiuresis.
Limit correction to 8 to 10 mmol/L in 24 hours to avoid osmotic demyelination.
Check sodium at baseline and around two weeks when starting these drugs in an older patient.
explanation.pearls: Mirtazapine and agomelatine carry the lowest reported risk of drug induced hyponatraemia among the antidepressants, which makes one of them the practical choice when depression still needs treating after a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor has caused it.

subtopic_detail: choosing between behavioural and pharmacological treatment for long standing sleep onset difficulty maintained by compensatory habits
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 39-year-old teacher who has had difficulty falling asleep for the past 14 months, most nights of the week. She takes about 90 minutes to get to sleep and feels unrefreshed and irritable during the day.

Her sleep diary shows she goes to bed at 9 pm to give herself the best chance, stays in bed reading on her phone until she feels sleepy, gets up at 6.30 am, and naps for 40 minutes most afternoons. She drinks one coffee at breakfast and none after midday. She has no snoring or witnessed apnoeas and her partner confirms this, no restless legs, and no low mood, anhedonia or anxiety on direct questioning. Her thyroid function and full blood count are within normal limits and she takes no regular medication. She asks for something to help her sleep.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 24, Mallampati class 1, no goitre
data_table.Sleep diary: Bed at 9 pm, sleep onset latency about 90 minutes, rise at 6.30 am, afternoon nap of about 40 minutes most days, total sleep time about 6 hours in 9.5 hours in bed
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid function and full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What would you recommend as first line treatment?

options.text: Prescribe temazepam 10 mg at night for two weeks with a plan to review and taper
options.rationale: Short term hypnotics have a place for acute situational insomnia but do not address maintaining behaviours, and tolerance plus rebound insomnia commonly follow in chronic insomnia of 14 months duration. The near pair distinction is duration: this is chronic rather than acute, which changes the first line answer. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Prescribe modified release melatonin 2 mg nightly for thirteen weeks with review at completion
options.rationale: Modified release melatonin is subsidised for primary insomnia in adults aged 55 and over, where age related decline in endogenous secretion is the rationale, and she is well below that age. Its effect size on sleep onset latency is modest even in the indicated population. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Hypnotics and Sedatives)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook: Hypnotics and Sedatives

options.text: Prescribe low dose amitriptyline 10 mg at night and review the response in four weeks
options.rationale: Sedating antidepressants are sometimes used off label for sleep but carry anticholinergic burden, daytime sedation and weight gain, with limited evidence in the absence of depression. She has no depressive symptoms on direct questioning, which removes the indication that would justify the class. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Arrange overnight polysomnography before deciding on treatment for her sleep difficulty
options.rationale: Sleep studies are indicated when a specific sleep disorder such as obstructive sleep apnoea, periodic limb movement disorder or narcolepsy is suspected, and none of those features is present with a normal body mass index and no snoring. Routine polysomnography in uncomplicated insomnia changes neither the diagnosis nor the treatment. (Source: RACGP: Management of Chronic Insomnia)

options.text: Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia including stimulus control and sleep restriction
options.rationale: Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia is first line for chronic insomnia in every major guideline and produces benefits that persist after treatment ends, unlike hypnotics whose effect stops with the drug. Her diary shows the exact maintaining behaviours the therapy targets, namely excessive time in bed, using the bed for wakeful activity, and daytime napping that erodes sleep pressure. (Source: RACGP: Management of Chronic Insomnia)

explanation.summary: Chronic insomnia is defined by difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep on at least three nights per week for at least three months with a daytime consequence, and it is best understood through a model in which a precipitating stressor is replaced over time by perpetuating behaviours that outlast it. Those behaviours are precisely the compensations that feel most sensible to the patient: going to bed earlier, staying in bed longer, napping, and using the bed as a place to wait for sleep. Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia bundles stimulus control, sleep restriction, cognitive restructuring of sleep related beliefs, and relaxation, and it is delivered face to face, in groups, or through validated digital programmes which have made access far more practical. Its effect is comparable to hypnotics in the short term and clearly superior beyond a few weeks, since the gains persist once treatment ends. Hypnotics retain a role for short term situational insomnia and as a bridge, but they are not the answer to a problem that has lasted more than a year.
key_points: Chronic insomnia requires symptoms on three or more nights weekly for three months with daytime impact.
Perpetuating behaviours include extended time in bed, napping and wakeful activity in bed.
Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia is first line and its benefit persists after treatment stops.
Sleep restriction works by consolidating sleep through increased homeostatic pressure, not by reducing total sleep.
Polysomnography is reserved for suspected apnoea, limb movement disorder or narcolepsy.
explanation.pearls: Sleep restriction starts by setting time in bed to the average total sleep time from the diary, with a floor of five hours, and time in bed is extended by 15 minutes each week once sleep efficiency exceeds 85 per cent.

sources.label: Australian Medicines Handbook: Hypnotics and Sedatives

subtopic_detail: distinguishing a persistent grief reaction from a depressive episode fourteen months after a bereavement
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 58-year-old woman referred 14 months after her adult son died in a workplace accident. She describes an intense daily yearning for him, spends two to three hours most days looking at his photographs, and has kept his bedroom exactly as it was.

She avoids driving past the road to his workplace and has stopped seeing the friends they had in common because it feels disloyal. She says she cannot accept that he is gone and feels that part of herself died with him. When asked directly, she says her appetite is normal, she is sleeping about seven hours, she still enjoys gardening and her grandchildren's visits, and she has no thoughts of harming herself. She feels no guilt about anything other than not having collected him from work that day, and there is no psychomotor retardation on examination.

data_table.Examination: Tearful when discussing her son, reactive affect, no psychomotor retardation, cognition intact
data_table.Symptoms: Intense daily yearning, preoccupation with the deceased, identity disruption, avoidance of reminders, all present for 14 months
data_table.Negative findings: Appetite and sleep preserved, anhedonia absent with retained enjoyment of gardening and grandchildren, no pervasive guilt, no suicidal ideation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer for grief focused psychotherapy targeting the loss and the avoidance behaviours
options.rationale: Persistent intense yearning with identity disruption, inability to accept the death and avoidance of reminders, present daily beyond 12 months and causing impairment, is prolonged grief disorder, and targeted grief focused psychotherapy is the treatment with the strongest evidence. It outperforms both generic supportive counselling and antidepressant monotherapy in randomised trials of this specific presentation. (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Start an antidepressant at a therapeutic dose and review the response in four to six weeks
options.rationale: Her sleep, appetite and capacity for enjoyment are preserved and there is no pervasive guilt, which means she does not meet criteria for a depressive episode, and antidepressant monotherapy does not reliably reduce grief severity in trials. Medication is added when a comorbid depressive or anxiety disorder is present, which is the near pair distinction being tested. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Reassure her that this is a normal grief reaction and review again in a further six months
options.rationale: Uncomplicated grief softens over the first year so that the person can hold the loss alongside ordinary life, whereas her yearning remains at daily intensity at 14 months with active avoidance narrowing her world. Normalising it withholds a treatment that works and risks a further six months of entrenchment. (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Prescribe a short course of a benzodiazepine to reduce distress when she visits his bedroom
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines do not improve grief outcomes and there is evidence that early use after bereavement is associated with worse trajectories, partly because they blunt the emotional processing that recovery requires. They also reinforce the avoidance that is maintaining her symptoms. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Refer for eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing to treat the traumatic circumstances of the death
options.rationale: This is an established treatment for post-traumatic stress disorder, and it would be appropriate if she had intrusive re-experiencing, hyperarousal and nightmares of the event, which she does not describe. Her avoidance is of reminders of the person rather than of a witnessed traumatic scene, which is the feature separating the two conditions. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Prolonged grief disorder was added to the major diagnostic systems to name a presentation that is neither ordinary bereavement nor a depressive episode, and it affects roughly 7 to 10 per cent of bereaved adults, with higher rates after sudden, violent or unexpected deaths and after the loss of a child. The diagnosis requires persistent intense yearning or preoccupation with the deceased, together with symptoms such as identity disruption, disbelief, avoidance of reminders, emotional numbness, a sense that life is meaningless and difficulty re-engaging, present most days and causing impairment beyond 12 months in adults. Distinguishing it from major depression matters because the treatments differ: grief is oriented around the lost person with preserved capacity for pleasure elsewhere, while depression is pervasive with anhedonia, guilt and neurovegetative change. The evidence favours structured grief focused psychotherapy, which combines exposure to avoided reminders with work on restoring goals and relationships, over medication alone. Antidepressants are reserved for comorbid depression or anxiety rather than for the grief itself.
key_points: The adult time criterion is symptoms persisting beyond 12 months from the death.
Yearning and preoccupation centred on the deceased is the core feature, not pervasive low mood.
Preserved appetite, sleep and capacity for enjoyment argue against a comorbid depressive episode.
Grief focused psychotherapy outperforms supportive counselling and antidepressant monotherapy.
Sudden, violent or unexpected deaths and the loss of a child carry the highest risk.
explanation.pearls: Avoidance is the treatment target that most reliably predicts response: keeping a room unchanged and avoiding shared friends prevents the repeated exposure through which the loss becomes tolerable, and grief focused therapy works largely by reversing exactly those two behaviours.

sources.label: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

subtopic_detail: recognising a motor syndrome mistaken for worsening psychosis when antipsychotic escalation has made it worse
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar called to an inpatient unit to review a 24-year-old man admitted eight days ago with a relapse of schizophrenia. His olanzapine was increased from 10 mg to 20 mg daily four days ago because the team felt he was becoming more withdrawn.

The nursing staff report he has stopped speaking entirely over the past 48 hours, is eating only when food is placed in his mouth, and has been standing by the window for long periods. When you examine him he does not respond to questions, resists passive movement of his arm with force that matches your own, and when you lift his forearm above the bed it stays where you place it for over a minute. He repeats the last few words of your sentence back to you twice. He is afebrile with no rigidity, no tremor and no diaphoresis, and his creatine kinase is 180 U/L (60 to 220).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 98 per cent in air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Mute, immobile with periods of maintained posture, waxy flexibility, gegenhalten on passive movement, echolalia, no rigidity or tremor, no diaphoresis
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 180 U/L (60 to 220), white cell count and C reactive protein within normal limits, sodium and calcium within normal limits
data_table.Medication: Olanzapine increased from 10 mg to 20 mg daily four days ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence nasogastric feeding and reassess the mental state after nutrition is established
options.rationale: Attention to nutrition, hydration and thromboprophylaxis is genuinely part of supportive care in a patient who is not eating, but it addresses a complication rather than the syndrome. Treating the catatonia is usually what restores oral intake within a day or two. (Source: RANZCP: Catatonia Guidance)

options.text: Withhold the olanzapine and give a lorazepam challenge with close observation of the response
options.rationale: Mutism, immobility, posturing, waxy flexibility, gegenhalten and echolalia together make up a catatonic syndrome, and a parenteral lorazepam challenge is both the diagnostic test and the first line treatment, with a substantial response typically seen within minutes to hours. Antipsychotic exposure can precipitate and worsen catatonia and raises the risk of progression to the malignant form, so it is withheld while the benzodiazepine is trialled. (Source: RANZCP: Catatonia Guidance)

options.text: Increase the olanzapine further to 30 mg daily to treat the worsening negative symptoms
options.rationale: Reading immobility and mutism as negative symptoms and escalating the antipsychotic is the central anti-pattern of this presentation, and the deterioration that followed the last increase is the clue that it is already happening. Further dopamine blockade risks converting simple catatonia into the malignant form. (Source: RANZCP: Catatonia Guidance)

options.text: Start intravenous dantrolene with bromocriptine and transfer to a high dependency bed
options.rationale: This is the treatment for neuroleptic malignant syndrome, which is the important near pair, but that diagnosis requires fever, lead pipe rigidity, autonomic instability and a markedly raised creatine kinase, none of which is present here. Waxy flexibility and gegenhalten are features of catatonia rather than of the rigidity of neuroleptic malignant syndrome. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Arrange urgent magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and lumbar puncture before any treatment
options.rationale: Investigation for an organic cause including autoimmune encephalitis is appropriate in a first presentation or where there are neurological signs, fever or cognitive fluctuation, and it may still be pursued in parallel. It should not delay a lorazepam challenge that is low risk and may produce a diagnostic response within the hour. (Source: RANZCP: Catatonia Guidance)

explanation.summary: Catatonia is a motor dysregulation syndrome that occurs across psychiatric and medical conditions, most commonly with mood disorders rather than schizophrenia despite its historical association, and also with autoimmune encephalitis, metabolic derangement and drug withdrawal. It is substantially underdiagnosed because its features are read as negative symptoms, depression or non compliance, and the Bush Francis Catatonia Rating Scale exists to make the examination systematic. Two or more of the recognised signs, including stupor, mutism, negativism, posturing, waxy flexibility, echolalia, echopraxia, stereotypy and automatic obedience, establish the diagnosis. Benzodiazepines are first line, with lorazepam producing a response in a majority of cases, and electroconvulsive therapy is the definitive treatment for those who do not respond and for malignant catatonia. Malignant catatonia adds fever and autonomic instability and overlaps clinically with neuroleptic malignant syndrome, with antipsychotics contraindicated in both.
key_points: Two or more catatonic signs establish the diagnosis; the Bush Francis scale structures the examination.
Mood disorders are the commonest psychiatric substrate, not schizophrenia.
A parenteral lorazepam challenge serves as both diagnostic test and first line treatment.
Antipsychotics can precipitate or worsen catatonia and risk progression to the malignant form.
Electroconvulsive therapy is definitive for benzodiazepine non response and for malignant catatonia.
explanation.pearls: A lorazepam challenge uses 1 to 2 mg parenterally with the catatonic signs re-scored at 5 to 10 minutes, and a partial response justifies proceeding to regular dosing that often reaches 8 to 16 mg daily without the sedation that those doses would cause in a non catatonic patient.
